game_mammals: Deer only. A 'salvageable deer' is one killed by a motor vehicle collision on a Massachusetts way, or one seriously injured in a collision and then killed at the scene by a law enforcement officer. The driver or a passenger of the striking vehicle may salvage it if they are domiciled in Massachusetts. The regulation does not cover moose, bear or other mammals.
game_birds: Not covered. 321 CMR 2.04 applies only to deer, and no salvage provision for wild turkey or upland birds was found, so possessing them would need separate authorization. Migratory birds (waterfowl, doves, woodcock) are federally protected under the MBTA and cannot be possessed without a federal permit.
permit_process: On taking possession, immediately notify the Office of Law Enforcement (Environmental Police) of the intent to salvage, giving name, address, and the date, time and place of the kill. If that office cannot be reached, notify local police or the nearest State Police barracks and ask that the incident be logged. Then bring the carcass to a MassWildlife or OLE office, or to an Environmental Police Officer at a location the officer names. The officer attaches a seal and issues a free salvage permit.
timing: Notify immediately on taking possession. The carcass must be presented for sealing and the permit within 24 hours of the kill. The seal stays on until the deer is butchered, and the permit is kept until all edible parts are consumed.
excluded_species: All species other than deer, which the regulation does not cover. Non-residents and people who were not in the striking vehicle may not take a deer themselves.
sale_of_parts: Prohibited. No sale, barter or exchange for payment. The person may keep the head, hide, hooves and shinbones for personal use.
other_restrictions: Massachusetts domicile is required. If the eligible person declines the deer, an Environmental Police Officer may give it to an approved nonprofit or to another Massachusetts-domiciled person, under a permit in the recipient's name. Inedible deer must be buried or incinerated.
statute_or_reg: 321 CMR 2.04 (Salvage, Disposition and Possession of Deer Killed by Means Other than by Sport Hunting)
agency: Massachusetts Division of Fisheries and Wildlife (MassWildlife) / Office of Law Enforcement (Massachusetts Environmental Police)
notes: The regulation's text was confirmed. No 2025-2026 changes were found.

game_mammals: Deer: get a salvage tag, or promptly notify the DNR or local law enforcement by phone or on the DNR website (a driver may tell 9-1-1 they intend to keep it). The DNR now runs a free online roadkill salvage permit, and current guidance says the permit is needed to possess the animal. Spotted fawns are excluded. Bear: salvage tag required, and cubs are excluded. Elk and moose are excluded. Small game mammals and some furbearers (beaver, coyote, fox, mink, muskrat, opossum, raccoon, skunk, weasel) need a written record kept with the animal.
game_birds: Wild turkey is expressly excluded. So are ducks, geese, brant, coot, snipe, woodcock, sora and Virginia rail, Florida gallinule and crow. 'Small game' (which appears to include pheasant, grouse and quail) may be salvaged with a written record, per the statute's small-game category. Migratory birds are also barred federally under the MBTA.
permit_process: Free DNR online salvage permit (Survey123 form linked from the DNR roadkill page), giving the date, location and intended use. The permit is emailed. Alternatively, a salvage tag from the DNR or the investigating officer. Questions go to the DNR Wildlife Division Permit Specialist at 517-284-6210.
timing: The statute requires 'prompt' notification or a tag and sets no fixed hourly deadline that was found. No seasonal limit was found.
excluded_species: Badger, bobcat, brant, coot, crow, cub bear, duck, elk, fisher, Florida gallinule, geese, marten, moose, otter, snipe, sora rail, spotted fawn deer, Virginia rail, wild turkey, wolf, woodcock, and endangered or threatened species (which fall under Part 365).
sale_of_parts: Not addressed in the salvage statute. Michigan law generally bars selling game, so assume sale is prohibited, though this was not confirmed.
other_restrictions: The driver has first priority. Salvage does not apply to anyone who intentionally kills or injures game with a vehicle. The DNR Director may suspend salvage in disease areas (CWD or bovine TB). Taking antlers from a roadkill deer without a permit is illegal possession.
statute_or_reg: MCL 324.40115 (added by 2014 PA 255, SB 613). The DNR also cites MCL 324.43539 and Wildlife Conservation Order section 4.5, which were not verified.
agency: Michigan Department of Natural Resources (DNR), Wildlife Division
notes: The statute text was confirmed. Details of the current online permit come from county and news pages that point to the DNR form, not from a DNR page read directly. Under the statute, notification alone may suffice for deer, but current DNR practice calls for the free online permit.

game_mammals: Deer: the driver who hit and killed a deer on a public road has first priority for a possession permit covering the whole animal, if the facts show it was not taken illegally. Otherwise any Minnesota resident may request one. Permits are also issued for bear and for small game such as rabbits and squirrels, per DNR and news reports.
game_birds: No bird-specific statute was found. Permits are reportedly issued for 'many other animals', so turkey or upland birds would be at the issuing officer's discretion (unconfirmed). Migratory birds cannot be possessed without a federal MBTA permit.
permit_process: Free possession permit from a DNR conservation officer, the State Patrol, a county sheriff or another law enforcement officer, usually at the scene. Permits are valid for 6 months. DNR enforcement lines: 888-646-6367 or 651-296-6157.
timing: The permit is valid for 6 months. No reporting deadline in hours was found, but the permit must be obtained before possessing or transporting the animal.
excluded_species: Not codified. Protected, threatened or endangered species presumably cannot be possessed, but this was not confirmed.
sale_of_parts: Not addressed on the DNR page. General Minnesota game laws restrict sale of wild animal meat, so assume sale is prohibited, though this was not confirmed.
other_restrictions: The road authority removes deer that are not salvaged. In CWD management zones, carcass movement restrictions apply: only certain parts may leave the zone, and whole carcasses must stay for testing. Possessing roadkill without a permit can bring misdemeanor charges.
statute_or_reg: Minn. Stat. 97A.502 (Deer killed by motor vehicles)
agency: Minnesota Department of Natural Resources (DNR), Enforcement Division
notes: The statute is deer-specific, while practice extends permits to other species. Residency is reported by secondary sources, not confirmed in the statute. The DNR page is dated.

game_mammals: No Mississippi statute or MDWFP regulation that specifically authorizes or regulates salvaging road-killed deer was found. Secondary sources say game animals may be collected without a permit, but they cite no official authority. Contact an MDWFP conservation officer before taking a road-killed deer.
game_birds: No specific rule was found. Migratory birds are federally protected under the MBTA. Wild turkey should not be possessed out of season without MDWFP authorization (assumed).
permit_process: No formal salvage permit was found. The recommended practice is to contact an MDWFP conservation officer or local law enforcement.
excluded_species: Endangered or protected species (federal and state). Out-of-season game possession may be an issue.
sale_of_parts: Sale of wild game meat is generally prohibited in Mississippi (assumed). Not confirmed for roadkill.
other_restrictions: Deer carcasses may not be dumped on roadsides; this is littering, with a fine of up to $250. Mississippi bans importing whole cervid carcasses from out of state because of CWD (40 Miss. Code R. 2-2.7). In-state CWD management zone carcass rules may apply.
statute_or_reg: None specific found. The CWD carcass import rule is 40 Miss. Code R. 2-2.7.
agency: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks (MDWFP)
notes: Secondary sources (legalclarity.org, animalofthings.com) claim salvage is allowed without a permit for 'game animals only', but they cite no official authority and contradict themselves. Treat the legal status as unverified.

game_mammals: Deer: a driver who hits a deer and wants to keep it must get authorization from a conservation agent; reports describe a free 'Wildlife Dispensation Permit'. Antlers taken from a road-killed deer still attached to the skull plate also need agent authorization, requested within 24 hours. No specific rules were found for other big game: elk are restricted, and black bear has a limited season.
game_birds: No road-killed turkey rule was found. Possessing any wildlife found dead generally needs agent authorization under the Wildlife Code. Migratory birds are barred federally under the MBTA.
permit_process: Contact the local MDC conservation agent, who issues a free written authorization (Wildlife Dispensation Permit).
timing: Report to an agent within 24 hours to receive possession authorization; MDC states this explicitly for antlered deer heads and road-killed deer.
excluded_species: Not specified. Endangered species and protected wildlife are presumably not authorized.
sale_of_parts: Not confirmed for roadkill. Shed antlers not attached to the skull may be bought and sold without authorization. Sale of wildlife meat is generally prohibited.
other_restrictions: CWD carcass movement and testing rules may apply in CWD management zones. Wildlife taken illegally cannot be possessed (3 CSR 10-4.141).
statute_or_reg: Wildlife Code of Missouri, 3 CSR 10. The exact roadkill or found-dead section was not confirmed; Chapter 10 (antlers) is referenced by MDC.
notes: The 24-hour agent-authorization rule comes from an MDC Conservationist Q&A (2009) and recent news reports. The exact current Code section was not verified.

game_mammals: Only white-tailed deer, mule deer, pronghorn antelope, elk and moose may be salvaged. Anyone may salvage, not just the driver, with a permit.
game_birds: Not allowed. Salvage is limited to the five big game species, so upland birds, turkey and waterfowl may not be salvaged (migratory birds are also barred federally under the MBTA).
permit_process: Free Vehicle-Killed Wildlife Salvage Permit, from on-scene law enforcement or online through FWP. The permit must be printed (an electronic copy on a phone is not accepted), signed and carried.
timing: Get the permit within 24 hours of taking possession. No seasonal limit.
excluded_species: All species other than deer, elk, moose and antelope, including bear, bighorn sheep, mountain goat, bison, furbearers and birds.
sale_of_parts: Prohibited. The meat must be used for human consumption (not bait) and may not be sold. The Montana Food Bank Network does not accept roadkill.
other_restrictions: The entire carcass, including entrails, must be removed from the roadway; field dressing is allowed only if all parts are taken away. The salvager may not kill an injured animal, but an officer may, after which it can be salvaged. Unusable parts must go to a legal disposal site, and dumping within 200 yards of a road or public property is illegal. Hunting carcass tags may not be used on roadkill. CWD carcass transport rules may also apply (not stated on the FWP page).
notes: Confirmed on the official FWP page.

game_mammals: Deer, antelope and elk killed on a roadway by a vehicle may be possessed with a salvage permit or tag. Possession priority: the person in the accident, then public institutions, then nonprofits, then other individuals. The driver may field dress the animal at the scene and take it home.
game_birds: No roadkill salvage provision for birds. Found-dead parts of upland game birds may be possessed but not sold, and feathers may not bear shot marks. Wild turkey is not specifically addressed. Migratory birds are barred federally under the MBTA.
permit_process: Notify Nebraska Game and Parks. A Conservation Officer or designee tags the carcass with a two-part salvage tag: Part 1 goes to the district office, and Part 2 stays with the carcass or meat.
timing: Notify within 24 hours of picking up the carcass. The officer tags it within 48 hours of notification. The permit is valid for up to 90 days.
excluded_species: All big game other than deer, antelope and elk (e.g., bighorn sheep, mountain lion), plus protected and endangered species. Any carcass showing evidence of being shot.
sale_of_parts: Selling or trading meat is prohibited. The hide, hair, hooves, bones, horns and antlers of roadkill deer, antelope or elk may be sold. Processed meat may be given away with a receipt showing the permit information.
other_restrictions: Nebraska residents only. Individuals may hold only one roadkill carcass at a time. No processing for preservation before the permit is obtained.
notes: Confirmed from the regulation text on Cornell LII. No Game and Parks web page was read directly.

game_mammals: Newly authorized. SB 215 (2025), signed May 31, 2025 as Statutes of Nevada 2025, ch. 184, directs the Board of Wildlife Commissioners to adopt regulations for free NDOW wildlife salvage permits covering wildlife killed in vehicle collisions. It exempts permit holders from the tag requirements of NRS 502.150 and the closed-season possession ban of NRS 503.030. The implementing Commission General Regulation (CGR 5.27) was being revised in mid-2026; the draft excludes black bear.
game_birds: The bill text sets no species limit. The draft CGR 5.27 excludes crows. Upland bird and turkey eligibility under the final regulation is unconfirmed. Migratory birds are barred federally under the MBTA.
permit_process: Free NDOW wildlife salvage permit under Commission regulation. The application method (online or officer) is not confirmed.
timing: The draft CGR 5.27 revision (August 2026) changes the reporting or permit deadline from 48 hours to '2 business days'. The final adopted text is unconfirmed.
excluded_species: Draft: black bear and crow. The Commission may halt salvage permits if CWD is detected in Nevada. Protected and endangered species are presumably excluded.
sale_of_parts: Not addressed in SB 215. The failed 2021 bill (AB 299) would have banned sale. Unconfirmed under the current regulation.
other_restrictions: Salvage permits may be suspended if CWD is detected in Nevada. Other conditions (whole-carcass removal, restricted highways) are unconfirmed for the final regulation.
statute_or_reg: SB 215 (2025), Statutes of Nevada 2025, ch. 184 (new section in NRS ch. 501; amends NRS 502.150 and 503.030); Commission General Regulation 5.27 (wildlife salvage permit), under revision
agency: Nevada Department of Wildlife (NDOW) / Board of Wildlife Commissioners
notes: This is a recent change: Nevada was a long-time holdout, and AB 299 (2021) failed. SB 215 passed both chambers unanimously and was signed May 31, 2025. The implementing regulation's details came from an August 2026 news summary of a county advisory board vote and are not final; check NDOW for the adopted CGR 5.27.

game_mammals: New Hampshire residents may possess wildlife accidentally killed by a motor vehicle with an N.H. Wildlife Permit for Wildlife Accidentally Killed by Motor Vehicle. This commonly covers deer, moose and bear. The driver has priority, per secondary sources.
game_birds: The rule covers 'wildlife' generally. Wild turkey is reportedly salvageable under the same permit (secondary source). Migratory birds cannot be possessed without a federal MBTA permit.
permit_process: Complete the department form, available from a conservation officer or any NH law enforcement officer, and submit it to a conservation officer for approval. If no officer is available, call Fish and Game dispatch at 603-271-3361 for instructions. Keep the approved copy with the meat. Moose and other protected wildlife may also need a Special Wildlife Permit (Fis 1102.01).
timing: The permit is valid for 6 months and can be extended once for another 6 months. No specific hours-based deadline was found.
excluded_species: Not enumerated in the rule. Threatened or endangered species presumably cannot be possessed.
sale_of_parts: Not addressed. Assume sale is prohibited (unconfirmed).
other_restrictions: New Hampshire residents only. The applicant acknowledges receiving the animal and releases the department from liability for whether it is safe to eat.
statute_or_reg: N.H. Admin. Rules Fis 1102.02 (also Fis 1102.01 for moose and protected wildlife). The underlying RSA was not confirmed.
agency: New Hampshire Fish and Game Department
notes: The rule text was confirmed (effective 2004, amended 2011). Species scope and turkey coverage come from secondary sources.

game_mammals: Deer only. A person may possess a deer accidentally killed in a motor vehicle collision, or one so badly injured it had to be killed, with a possession permit from State or municipal police.
game_birds: Not covered. New Jersey's roadkill provision applies only to deer, so turkey, pheasant and other birds may not be salvaged under it. Migratory birds are barred federally under the MBTA.
permit_process: Report the collision to police promptly. State or municipal police issue a possession permit on a Division of Fish and Wildlife form. Butchers may also require registration with the state by phone or online, with a confirmation number, before processing.
timing: Report promptly to police. The permit is valid for 90 days from issue.
excluded_species: All species other than deer, including bear.
sale_of_parts: Not addressed. The permit allows keeping the deer for consumption or transferring it to another person for that purpose. Sale is presumed prohibited (unconfirmed).
other_restrictions: The collision must be reported to police. Permits come from the police department of the municipality where the deer was found.
agency: New Jersey Division of Fish and Wildlife (NJDEP); permits issued by State or municipal police
notes: The regulation text was confirmed (current through June 2025). The state-registration step for butchers comes from a news report (NJ101.5).
